near_miss.lead: Maternal relatives and gifts of clothing
near_miss.why_not: Irish maternal aunt supplies clothes, whereas Helen gives a bridal garment to be stored by the mother. Mother is cognate but neither the giver relationship nor the wording matches; other partners give ordinary genealogy or marriage negotiations.

near_miss.lead: Cows and women as totality of recovered spoils
near_miss.why_not: Irish promises to restore every cow and woman after victory; Norse lists men, women, children and cattle as slaughter victims. Vedic cow carrying calf is a riddle, not recovery of captives. No distinctive matching cognate phrase in the slab.

near_miss.lead: Protection of the house against fire
near_miss.why_not: Irish storytelling promises that fire will not burn a new house; Norse narrates setting a dry wooden building on fire. Neither the predicate nor fire noun supplies a matching inherited protective formula.

near_miss.lead: Father, brother, mother in marriage rules
near_miss.why_not: The Norse list specifies marriage guardians; AV 1.14 binds a woman to the house of mother, brother or father. Comparable social domain and cognate kin terms, but this is an expected family enumeration, with no distinctive shared construction beyond ordinary kinship.

Irish deug suain is a sleep potion, whereas Norse drunken sleep is narrated through intoxication and falling asleep, and the Sanskrit army sleeps from exhaustion. Shared sleep root does not yield a corresponding collocation.

Norse í heyranda hljóði describes a public legal proclamation; Greek ἀκοῇ κλύειν is paired with seeing in a divine epiphany. The cognate hljóð/κλύειν material has different syntactic functions and no shared legal or poetic figure.

search_lead.cognate: Norse verk and Greek ἔργον continue *werg̑-; orð and ἔπος are lexical replacements rather than an exact cognate pair.
search_lead.argument: Norse með orðum eða verkum and Homeric instrumental ἢ ἔπει ἢ ἔργῳ express the speech/action merism; Il. 11.703 applies it to anger at words and deeds, closer to the Norse injury clause. A plausible traditional merism, but the medieval Christmas-peace law could inherit Christian or wider European usage, so PIE continuity remains unproven. Search found a better partner than the unrelated sacrifice verse in this bundle. The same injury merism also occurs in slab bundle BS-bf87a.

near_miss.why_not: A Homeric speech/action merism was found by searches for orð + verk and ἔπος + ἔργον, and is recorded as a search lead. The slab partner AV 11.1.s30 concerns a sacrifice obtaining benefits and does not supply that merism.

The slab Latin partner has oculorum lumine operto, closing the eyes in an erotic context, rather than birth. Searches for φῶς + ἔρχομαι and lux + edo gave no hits; lumen + ora located genuine birth parallels, recorded separately as a search lead.

The Norse speaker likens his human enemy to a thick-necked serpent; the Greek partner argues over military leadership. No matching serpent-slaying collocation, and the Norse uses fall/die rather than a cognate inherited slaying predicate.

near_miss.lead: Bright day departing / dark night arriving
near_miss.why_not: The Irish day/night contrast is clear, but both Norse partners concern mounting horses and riding over mountains. Shared movement alone does not transmit the figure.

Another attestation of the Norse formula examined in BS-02a3e; the Latin partner is a cattle medicine prescription. No two-branch slab match. External Homeric comparison is recorded under the first occurrence.

The slab Greek wolf is the personal name Lykos. Latin lupus + auris returned no hits; a cross-corpus wolf + ear root search found the same Finnboga proverb in another edition and Greek holding-a-wolf-by-the-ears proverbs (Polybius 30.20.8 and Plutarch 802d). Seeing the ears and grasping them are different images. Other returned hits were names or the Aesopic ears-versus-stomach fable, not this proverb.

near_miss.lead: God favourable if truthful, angry if lying
near_miss.why_not: The Russian partner reports thunder, not an oath. Latin corpus search found Plautus Amphitruo 933–936, asking Jupiter to be angry if the speaker deceives and responding with propitius. This is a comparable conditional oath, but no distinctive shared cognate collocation supports inheritance over ordinary oath-making or later transmission in a Christian law.
Irish sanctions Sunday grinding with a fine; Hittite lists ritual food quantities including meal. Cognate grinding vocabulary is not a shared formula or congruent ritual action.
Norse describes the wealth of a man named Úlfr; the chronicle compares Igor to a wolf seizing and plundering. The apparent image is caused by a personal-name mapping.

Norse Ulfr beit ennibjalfa occurs in a combat stanza, with the next line describing an edge entering legs. Sanskrit bhittvā śarīrāṇi vṛkāṇām describes breaking through wolves’ bodies. Even if the Norse wolf is read metaphorically, wolf is subject there and possessor of the affected bodies in Sanskrit; no shared predicate-object formula survives.

near_miss.lead: Marriage controlled by father, brother, mother
near_miss.why_not: Recurrent kinship list from BS-657aa; the Atharvavedic woman bound to the family home is contextually suggestive but the cognate terms name expected guardians. The Irish partner adds wider social relationships rather than a distinctive shared marriage formula.

Irish fiadach feda is game of the wood, with feda genitive singular of fid; the Welsh partner describes hunting and preparing dogs and a net but lacks the corresponding cognate noun phrase. Norse partners concern court positions and settlement of rulership.

search_lead.cognate: Norse ljós and Latin lumen continue the *leuk- light family; koma and Latin exit/edant/profudit are different motion or production predicates.
search_lead.argument: The Norse inheritance rule requires a conceived child to come alive into light and be baptized. Lucretius uses motion into the regions of light for birth, explicitly from the maternal womb at 5.224–225. This is a semantic and phraseological lead with a cognate light noun, not a demonstrated reconstruction: the visual metaphor is natural and the Christian legal setting permits later transmission. The slab Latin partner instead concerns closed eyes.
